t: 3766. Minimum Operations to Make Binary Palindrome
o: For each number we may increment or decrement it, paying 1 per step, until its binary form (no leading zeros) reads the same forwards and backwards; report the minimal cost per element. E.g. 2 (10) -> 3 (11) costs 1, 4 (100) -> 3 (11) costs 1, 12 (1100) -> 15 (1111) costs 3. Since nums[i] <= 5000, all relevant palindromes fit in 13 bits (up to 8191). Precomputing every binary palindrome once and answering each query by binary search over neighbors gives an O(M log M + Q log M) solution where M is the palindrome count (a few hundred).
k: Binary palindromes are sparse: generating them by mirroring bit halves yields only O(sqrt(V)) candidates up to V.
The nearest palindrome to x is one of its sorted-list neighbors, found by binary search.
Values up to 5000 need palindromes up to 13 bits (8191) to cover the 'round up' case.

a.n: Approach 1: Precompute all palindromes + binary search
a.i: Enumerate each bit-length L from 1 to 13, take every possible first half, mirror it (sharing or not sharing the middle bit) to form a palindrome, collect and sort them. Each query is answered by the closer of the two surrounding palindromes.
s: Generate all binary palindromes with up to 13 bits by mirroring halves; sort the list.
For each x, binary search for the first palindrome >= x.
Answer with min(pal[idx] - x, x - pal[idx-1]).
a.t: O(M + Q log M) - generating/sorting ~few hundred palindromes once, then a binary search per query

a.i: Without a global table, take x's binary string, mirror its first half (rounded both ways, +/-1 on the half) to synthesize the few candidate palindromes of the same length, and take the closest. Only O(log x) candidates per query, no preprocessing.
s: Write x in binary; let L be its length.
Build candidates by mirroring the ceil(L/2)-bit and floor(L/2)-bit prefixes, also with the prefix incremented/decremented (same length only).
a.t: O(Q log V) - a constant number of length-preserving mirror candidates per query

w: Prefer Approach 1 for simplicity and robustness; Approach 2 shines if memory is tight or values are huge. Pitfalls: forgetting palindromes above the maximum query value (13 bits for 5000), mirroring with the wrong parity (odd lengths share the middle bit), and dropping leading zeros incorrectly. Follow-up: queries up to 1e18 (same ideas, 63 bits), or count palindromes in a range.
